Seated disputants in orange and green turn to one another in the middle ground; a robed man in pale yellow stands full-length at center; the kneeling couple at the right raise clasped hands. The meander-patterned pavement and left colonnade lock the space in perspective, and a strip of blue sky opens above the rotunda.
entries.quality: Set beside its sibling sheet, this pull is bluer and evener, and the gain is spatial — the pavement, steps, and rotunda click into one continuous depth. What it trades away is heat: Paul's red mantle no longer dominates, so the crowd competes with its own architecture a little more than it should.

entries.title: The School of Athens
entries.shown: After Raphael's fresco, rendered as a duotone engraving in deep violet-blue on cream: Plato and Aristotle walk forward under the great coffered barrel vaults, flanked by the full company — Pythagoras writing at the lower left, Heraclitus brooding at his block, Diogenes sprawled on the steps, Euclid bending over his slate at the right. Niched statues of Apollo and Minerva stand above the crowd, and a painted dado of grisaille panels and caryatids runs beneath. The receding arches stack toward a bright open sky at the center.
entries.quality: The engraver's real achievement is the vault — the diminishing coffers and Greek-key soffits carry the fresco's architecture into pure line without losing its pull toward the light. At this reduction the fifty-odd philosophers become a frieze of attitudes rather than portraits, which the print seems to accept; the ornamental border and dado are finished with a miniaturist's patience.

entries.title: The School of Athens, with Touches of Color
entries.shown: The same composition after Raphael's fresco, here with sparing hand-color laid over the blue engraving: a yellow mantle on a figure right of center, muted reds and violets scattered through the crowd. Plato and Aristotle advance beneath the coffered vaults between the statue niches; Pythagoras, Diogenes on the steps, and the geometers at the right hold their stations; the grisaille dado with its standing figures closes the base of the sheet.
entries.quality: The added color is applied like accents in a margin — enough to lead the eye to the central pair and the sprawled Diogenes without breaking the engraving's tonal unity. It is the more legible of the two pulls, though the tinting is casual in the right-hand group, where a red robe floats free of its drawing.

entries.title: The Transfiguration
entries.shown: After Raphael's last altarpiece: Christ hovers in a burst of white cloud at the summit, arms raised, flanked by the floating figures of Moses and Elijah, while the three disciples sprawl dazzled on the mount below and two witnesses kneel at the far left. Beneath the hill the second scene crowds the foreground — the nine apostles gesturing and pointing upward at the left, and at the right the possessed boy, eyes rolled back, held by his father amid the kneeling woman in white and rose who pivots between the two groups. Light pours downward from the cloud.
entries.quality: The print keeps Raphael's double machine intact: the upper zone is left airy and pale so the lower tumult, hand-tinted in rose and green, presses against it exactly as the design demands. The engraved stippling of the dark hillside is the connective tissue and it holds; the boy's convulsion, the hardest passage in the original, arrives at earnest stiffness rather than terror.

entries.title: The Sacrifice of Isaac
entries.shown: After Rembrandt, printed in deep blue on cream: Isaac lies bound across the fagots in the foreground, bare-chested, his face covered entirely by Abraham's spread left hand as the old man turns his bearded face upward. The angel plunges in from the upper left, wings spread, one hand thrown up and the other gripping toward Abraham's arm; the loosed knife hangs falling in mid-air at the center of the sheet, above a horn and the smoking altar. A dark tree mass closes the right; a pale distance opens at the lower left.
entries.quality: The dramatic reading is Rembrandt's own — the hand smothering the boy's face, the knife caught between release and fall — and the duotone serves it, the ink night pressing in on the two reserved bodies. The suspended knife is the sheet's masterstroke of timing; the angel's second hand, oddly clawed, is where the drawing goes coarse.

entries.title: The Elephant in Eden
entries.shown: A dense pen-and-ink garden in blue line: an elephant, trunk raised, stands in a sunlit clearing at the center, framed between a huge shadowed tree trunk at the left, a curtain of cascading rock or foliage behind, and banks of scribbled shrubbery climbing the right edge. Dark cross-hatched masses close the lower corners; broad-leafed plants sprout in the foreground. The paper's bare cream makes the light of the clearing.
entries.quality: This takes the famous background beast of Rembrandt's Adam and Eve etching and lets it hold the stage alone, and the freedom of the line — loops, scribbles, crosshatch laid fast — is the pleasure of the sheet. It is atmosphere rather than anatomy: the elephant is a marvel of shorthand, but the surrounding vegetation dissolves into handwriting wherever the eye slows down.

entries.title: Christ Led Away
entries.shown: A hand-colored woodcut in the old German manner: Christ in a long pale robe, head bowed, is led at the wrists by a stooped man in green while an armored captain with a yellow-plumed helmet stands at the center gripping his sword hilt. Around them press five more figures — a green-robed elder with a staff at the left, a boy in red, soldiers in red at the right, one seen from behind with a sword at his belt — with a fence of pikes and spears rising behind. The ground is a flat dark band; the hatched sky opens to bare paper around the plume.
entries.quality: The block-book flatness is deliberate and well kept — figures in a single frieze, color confined to green, red, and one shout of yellow at the exact center of power. The bowed white figure of Christ, left almost unmarked amid the busy hatching, is the quietest and best decision on the sheet; the faces are stock types, as the idiom intends.

entries.title: Jacob Wrestling with the Angel
entries.shown: Two figures fill a night-blue field: the angel, upright in a white off-shoulder garment with great bronze-feathered wings spread across the top of the sheet, looks calmly down while one hand cups the back of Jacob's neck and the other braces against his hip. Jacob, dark-curled and bearded, in a red mantle, drives his weight into the angel's body, face pressed toward the shoulder, one bare leg thrust back for purchase. There is no ground and no horizon — only the hold.
entries.quality: Cropping the story to the clinch is the print's whole argument, and it wins: the wings make the architecture, the red and white make the struggle, and the angel's unhurried face against Jacob's straining back states the mismatch better than any landscape could. The flat blue field is fearless; only Jacob's rear leg, slightly boneless, betrays the drawing.

entries.title: Jacob Wrestling the Angel
entries.shown: Two figures fill the frame against a night-blue ground ruled with fine horizontal lines: a winged angel in a white shift, calm-faced, curls lit from above, and a bearded man in a red robe pressed against her body, his face turned up to hers. One of her hands cups the back of his neck, the other rests at his hip; his bare foot braces on a ledge at the bottom edge. The light gathers on her face and gown, and the eye travels from her downcast gaze to his open, straining mouth.
entries.quality: The print, after Rembrandt, understands that the subject is a hold, not a blow — the whole struggle is carried in two quiet hands, and the red robe is spent in one place, where the bodies meet. The spread wings are drawn with real feathered weight, though the angel's serenity is so complete she risks reading as unmoved rather than merciful.

entries.title: The Raising of Lazarus
entries.shown: In a cave dark enough to swallow most of the plate, Christ stands on a rock shelf with one arm thrown straight up, and below him at right a shrouded man lifts head and hand out of a stone grave. At left a knot of witnesses catches the light — an old man peering over Christ's shoulder, a young woman with both palms raised. On the cave wall hang a sword and sheath picked out in red and gold, the only bright objects in the upper half.
entries.quality: The plate keeps its nerve about darkness: perhaps four-fifths of it is worked black, and the few lit passages — the raised hand, the grave-cloth, the girl's face — do all the telling. The hung weapons at upper right are a fine Rembrandtesque touch of still life, though they pull the eye harder than the miracle strictly allows.

entries.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
entries.shown: A ragged son kneels with his back to us, one shoe half off his blistered feet, while his father in a red mantle bends over him and lays both hands flat on his shoulders. Three onlookers keep their distance: a servant at a doorway, a seated man in a hat with folded hands, and a tall bearded elder in a red cloak leaning on a staff at right. A woman watches from a dark arched window, and vine leaves close the scene at the top corner.
entries.quality: Cut in the manner of a woodblock after Rembrandt's design, the print puts its whole argument in the two pressed-down hands and the dirty soles turned toward us — the one detail Rembrandt himself insisted on. The flat duotone serves the composition well; the bystanders' faces are more summary than the drama of the drapery deserves.

entries.title: The Anointing of David
entries.shown: A ruined tower of Roman masonry rises through most of the plate, ivy climbing its broken face, its cornice touched with gold against a flat night-blue sky. Fallen column drums and cut stones litter the foreground path, and at its base two small figures in scarlet enact the scene — a bearded elder stands over a kneeling youth, hand extended above his head. A lone walker and further ruins hold the right distance.
entries.quality: An audacious inversion: the anointing is reduced to two red marks at the foot of an enormous ruin, and the spot color makes the tiny act command the whole architecture. The stonework is drawn with a topographer's patience; the human figures, at that scale, can afford to be little more than gesture — and are.

entries.title: Self-Portrait in a Red Gown
entries.shown: An old man in a deep crimson gown and matching soft cap turns three-quarters toward us against a blue ground striped with fine vertical hatching. His grey hair curls out beneath the cap, the face is heavily lined at brow and cheek, and his hands are folded together at the bottom of the frame. All the light sits in the face and the clasped hands; the gown holds the middle tones in long, simple folds.
entries.quality: After Rembrandt's late self-portraits, the print gets the essential thing right: the face is worked hardest where age is written — the pouched eyes, the furrowed forehead — while the costume is allowed to be broad and quiet. The steady vertical ground is a printmaker's economy that flatters the mass of the figure, though it gives the sitter none of the air Rembrandt's shadows breathe.

entries.title: Self-Portrait in a Flat Cap
entries.shown: A bust-length old man faces out from a square panel, wearing a wide flat cap banded in gold over abundant grey curls, a dark coat with a shawl collar, and a scarf touched with red at the throat. The ground behind him is a dense woven crosshatch of blue on cream. His eyes are large, level, and a little weary, and they hold the viewer directly.
entries.quality: This is the cleanest cutting in the set — every curl of hair and thread of the crosshatched ground is a deliberate stroke, and the two spot colors, gold at the cap and red at the throat, are placed with a jeweler's restraint. The woodcut convention flattens the great head slightly; what it loses in depth it repays in graphic force.

entries.title: The Storm on the Sea of Galilee
entries.shown: A fishing boat heels hard to port on a mountainous sea, its bow climbing a breaking wave that throws spray over the men hauling at the rigging. Sailors cling to the mast and gunwale; in the stern a calmer group gathers around a haloed figure while one man leans on the tiller. Two crew in yellow — one aloft in the shrouds, one hooded amidships — mark the diagonal from wave-crest to stern, and torn clouds open to pale sky at upper left.
entries.quality: The print, after Rembrandt's lost seascape, keeps the great diagonal of the original and renders water entirely by line — the wave at left is a genuinely persuasive piece of engraved foam. The division of the crew into panic forward and stillness aft survives the translation intact; the faces in the stern are too small to carry much beyond their grouping, and the composition carries them instead.

entries.title: The Supper at Emmaus
entries.shown: In an inn built into a great stone arch, Christ sits at a small draped table, hands at a loaf of bread, rays of light bursting from his head against the dark vault behind. One disciple sits with his back to us; the other, grey-bearded, leans in from the right and grips the table edge. A servant arrives from behind with a dish, unaware, and a dog sleeps by the chair leg at lower left.
entries.quality: The plate's best idea is borrowed honestly from Rembrandt: the enormous dark arch does the work of revelation, with the burst of engraved rays reading as light precisely because everything around it is patient crosshatch. The disciple's clenched hand on the table is the truest passage; the servant's obliviousness is nicely kept, though his anatomy is stiffer than his errand.

entries.title: The Apostle Thomas in His Study
entries.shown: A grey-bearded man in a fur-collared robe sits beside a writing table, a quill raised in his right hand and paused at his chin, a carpenter's square held loosely in his left against his knee. Papers, an inkwell, and a candlestick occupy the desk at left; behind him the wall divides into a black panel and a band of ruled grey light. A thin rim of yellow edges his hair and sleeve, as if from a source outside the frame.
entries.quality: A dignified scholar-portrait in the Rembrandt manner, its fur collar built from hundreds of short flicked strokes that genuinely read as pelt against the long calm lines of the robe. The suspended quill and the square give the sitter both thought and trade in one glance; the yellow contour light is a printer's flourish more decorative than optical.

entries.title: Titus Reading
entries.shown: A young man with loose shoulder-length curls sits in profile-turned-three-quarter view, eyes cast down on an open book held up in both hands, lips just parted as if reading aloud. He wears a dark coat with an embroidered cuff, and a wide-brimmed dark hat rings his head like a disc. The ground is close horizontal hatching; the light falls on his face, the page edges, and the reading hand.
entries.quality: After Rembrandt's portrait of his son, the print stakes everything on the absorbed face and wins — the lowered lids and open mouth are exactly the look of a boy lost in a page. The dark hat doubling as a halo is a happy graphic accident the cutter clearly noticed and kept; the embroidered cuff is lavished with more detail than the book it serves.

entries.title: The Payment of the Labourers in the Vineyard
entries.shown: In a tall, cavernous counting-room, a turbaned master in a red-fronted robe sits at a draped table, one hand at his chest, as a labourer leans across to protest and others crowd behind him examining coins in their palms. A clerk bends over ledgers at the far left under two glowing leaded windows; barrels, baggage, a hanging cage, and a chimney fill the shadowed right half, where a dog noses the floorboards.
entries.quality: The most pictorially ambitious plate of the group: it holds a full Rembrandt interior — window light, still-life clutter, deep aerial dark — in two inks and a single stroke of red at the master's breast, placed exactly where the parable's authority sits. The middle-ground figures counting their wage are drawn with real narrative intelligence; the far right is left so dark it functions as mass rather than room.

entries.title: Christ Washing the Feet of Peter
entries.shown: Christ kneels at a wide brass basin, sleeves pushed back, reaching toward the water, while Peter sits above him in a pale mantle, one hand raised in protest, the other opened at his chest. Ten disciples press around the candlelit table behind them, murmuring in pairs; a red cloak burns at the center of the group, and an open book stands between two candles on a stand at upper right.
entries.quality: After Rubens, and it shows in the good way: the two protagonists make a single interlocking diagonal of refusal and insistence, and the crowd behind is organized into legible conversations rather than a frieze of onlookers. The bare feet ringing the bottom of the frame are a quiet, correct touch. The single red cloak anchors the composition, though it crowns a bystander rather than either principal.

entries.title: The Temptation of Christ
entries.shown: On a bare mountain ledge above the clouds, a haloed Christ in pale rose-striped robes stands upright, one arm raised in dismissal, eyes turned away. Beside and below him a naked winged tempter strides toward the drop, torso twisting back, both arms flung open toward the kingdoms he is offering — which the frame pointedly declines to show. A crevasse splits the rock between their feet.
entries.quality: After Scheffer's painting, the print sharpens the contrast into pure line: Christ is all vertical drapery and stillness, the tempter all musculature and diagonal, and the empty ruled sky refuses the devil his panorama. The demon's écorché anatomy is the bravura passage; Christ's raised hand is drawn smaller and weaker than the gesture it must perform.

entries.title: The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, After Bernini
entries.shown: A print of Bernini's marble group in its chapel: the smiling angel, arrow lowered in one hand, lifts a fold of the saint's habit, while Teresa collapses backward on a bank of cloud, hooded head thrown back, one bare foot hanging free. Gilt rays pour down behind them from a hidden window, and the frame is closed by marbled pilasters, Corinthian capitals, and a small altar cross below.
entries.quality: The plate takes on the hardest problem in reproducing Bernini — rendering rays, marble, and cloud in flat ink — and solves it by letting the ruled gold shafts carry the light while the drapery is described as pure tumbling line. The convulsed habit is excellent; the two faces, where all of Bernini's scandal lives, are gentler and vaguer than the marble's.

entries.title: Head of Beethoven, After Bourdelle
entries.shown: A colossal bearded head, cut off at the neck, sits directly on a plain plinth against a ground of ruled horizontal lines. The brow is knotted, the deep-set eyes glare slightly leftward under heavy ridges, the hair piles in rough-modelled locks, and the mouth — the one touch of red in the print — is set hard within the beard. The lighting falls from the left, splitting the face into a lit and a shadowed half.
entries.quality: The engraving grasps what Bourdelle's bronze is about: the head as geology, all mass and pressure, with the modelling translated into contour hatching that follows the clay like a relief map. Reserving the sole red for the closed lips is a genuinely witty printer's decision — the music kept shut in the mouth — even if it lends the titan a faint theatricality.

entries.title: Beethoven, Tragic Mask, After Bourdelle
entries.shown: Another monumental Beethoven head after Bourdelle, seen slightly from below on a tall striped plinth, the neck ending in raw modelled clay. Here the face turns a few degrees right; one brow crushes down over the near eye while the far eye is lost in shadow, and the beard is worked into thick rope-like curls. A faint line of red again marks the lower lip; the ground is the same ruled blue field.
entries.quality: Of the two Beethoven plates this is the rougher and the stronger — the asymmetry of the crushed brow and the unhealed clay at the neck keep the head from settling into a monument, which is precisely Bourdelle's point. The hatching in the beard grows dense to the edge of clotting, a limit the cutter approaches but does not quite cross.

entries.title: David, After Donatello's Marble
entries.shown: A slender youth in a knotted cloak and draped skirt stands in contrapposto on a low plinth, one hand at his hip, the other hanging with a stone against his thigh, his weight on the leg beside the huge bearded head of Goliath lying at his feet. Behind him rises a niche of dark masonry with a strip of geometric inlay at the left edge; his face is smooth, wide-eyed, and unbothered.
entries.quality: The print renders Donatello's early marble David with an engraver's tact, keeping the adolescent slightness of the figure — the too-large hand at the hip, the boneless ease — that later Davids abandoned. Goliath's head, all tangled curls around the embedded stone, is the richest cutting in the plate; the flat niche behind serves the silhouette without competing.

entries.title: Saint George, After Donatello
entries.shown: A young knight in a cloak knotted at the throat stands frontally in a niche between two ornamented pilasters, both hands resting on a tall cross-blazoned shield set point-down before him. He wears armor at the arms and legs — the greaves picked out in gold — and his head turns slightly, brows level, jaw set, watching something beyond the frame. The niche behind is filled with diapered panels of dots and diamonds.
entries.quality: After the Orsanmichele marble, the plate preserves the one thing that matters in Donatello's George: the alert turn of the head over a perfectly braced stance, courage rendered as posture. The diapered background is transformed into a bold flat pattern that a woodcut can own outright rather than imitate stone; the gold on the greaves is arbitrary but handsome.

entries.title: A Panel from the Gates of Paradise
entries.shown: An engraved relief panel after Ghiberti: a deep arcaded courtyard of round arches and Corinthian pilasters, with robed figures conversing on the steps, a dog crossing the pavement at center, and a kneeling pair at the right where a slash of red opens behind an arch. Ornamental side pillars with single standing figures and floral bosses frame the scene like a doorjamb. The eye enters at the strollers on the stair and is drawn back through three receding archways.
entries.quality: The print's real subject is depth: parallel-hatched vaults stack one behind another with genuine conviction, and the two-tone economy — indigo line on cream, red held to one strategic slit — keeps the crowded stage legible. The figures, small and summarily drawn, are servants of the architecture rather than actors in it.

entries.title: The Gates of Paradise Seen from Below
entries.shown: A steep upward view of great bronze doors after Ghiberti, six relief panels visible in raking light, each a crowded landscape or architectural scene, with niched prophets and portrait roundels running down the ribbed frames between them. The gilt panels glow ochre against a night-black ground; the eye climbs the central pier from the lower medallions to the tilting cornice at top.
entries.quality: The dramatic worm's-eye foreshortening is the print's best decision — it restores to the doors the looming scale a straight-on plate would flatten — and the near-duotone of gold on blue-black reads as bronze more honestly than full color would. In the smallest reliefs the detail thickens into texture, and the individual stories dissolve.

entries.title: Laocoön and His Sons
entries.shown: An engraving after the antique group: the bearded father heaves back at center, head thrown up in agony, flanked by his two smaller sons, all three bound in coils of serpent picked out in red against ruled blue hatching. The figures stand on a stepped marble base before a flat sky of horizontal lines, with a dark hedge closing the middle distance.
entries.quality: The red serpents are a shrewd stroke — one spot color turns the whole tangle instantly legible and threads the three bodies into a single knot, while the woodcut-firm contours give the torsos real sculptural weight. The horizontally ruled sky is so mechanical it presses the group forward like a specimen against graph paper, which flatters clarity more than atmosphere.

entries.title: David in the Tribune
entries.shown: A low, close view of the standing David after Michelangelo, seen from beneath the pedestal so the body towers, the head turned left with the sling hand raised to the shoulder — where a single disc of yellow marks the stone. Behind him curve the paneled walls and coffered half-dome of a gallery apse, ruled in fine blue line with thin red seams tracing the moldings.
entries.quality: The print understands that David is an experience of looking up, and its perspective does the persuading: the legs lengthen, the head recedes, the dome bends overhead. The anatomy is confidently hatched, and the one drop of yellow at the hand is a witty economy, though the ruled architecture behind sits closer to draughtsman's diagram than to air.

entries.title: The Prodigal Son
entries.shown: A single nude male figure after Rodin, kneeling on a rough rock and flung upward from the hips, both arms stretched at full length toward the upper corners, head thrown back so only the underside of the jaw shows. He is a pale cream shape edged with a thin thread of gold, isolated against an unbroken field of deep night blue; the eye runs from the rock up the arched spine to the open hands.
entries.quality: This is the most abstemious print of the set and the strongest for it: one figure, one ground, and a silhouette that carries the whole cry in its diagonal. The interior hatching models the torso with real understanding of Rodin's strained musculature, while the vast empty blue does the emotional work a background would only dilute.

entries.title: The Thinker
entries.shown: The seated Thinker after Rodin in profile-quarter view, chin on the back of the bent right hand, elbow to knee, hunched on his rock above a stepped plinth. The bronze is rendered in deep blue with cream highlights raking across skull, shoulder, and shin, the whole figure rimmed by a rough red halo that separates him from the flat indigo ground.
entries.quality: The cream highlights are laid on like light on real bronze — the polish of the skull and the knuckles is observed, not invented — and the red keyline gives the mass a poster's punch without cheapening it. It is a print that trades Rodin's surface turbulence for graphic weight, and mostly wins the trade.

entries.title: The Winged Victory of Samothrace
entries.shown: The headless, armless Victory strides forward atop a stippled stone parapet, her single visible wing swept back and both legs pressing through wind-flattened drapery. Behind her a woodcut sky of ruled horizontals carries scrolled clouds; light falls from the left, leaving the wing dark and the gown's ridges pale. The eye rides the drapery's diagonal from hem to shoulder.
entries.quality: The engraver's whole intelligence has gone into the drapery, and it pays: the folds churn like water while the ruled sky behind stays dead calm, which is exactly the contrast the marble itself proposes. The stippled base is coarse next to that finesse, a pedestal in more senses than one.

entries.title: The Creation of the Animals
entries.shown: After Tintoretto: the Creator flies horizontally across the frame in a wind-filled red mantle, arm thrust out over a sea already boiling with fish, while flights of birds stream away to the left. Below and to the right the land fills with hares, deer, a porcupine, and, at the far edge, a white unicorn head among the trees; light radiates from the figure himself.
entries.quality: The print keeps Tintoretto's one great idea intact — creation as velocity, the Maker overtaking his own creatures — and the red cloak is the engine of the whole composition, the only saturated mass in a grisaille world. The animal inventory grows charmingly miscellaneous at the margins, more bestiary than ecosystem.

entries.title: Christ Appears on the Shore of Galilee
entries.shown: A white-robed figure edged in red stands on a pebbled shore, arms lifted toward a boat of small standing figures out on a still lake; a thin column of smoke rises from a coal fire at his feet straight up the left of the frame. Behind, dark headlands step back to a distant white town, the water ruled in fine horizontals that hold the boat's reflection.
entries.quality: The composition is patient in the manner of Tissot — the vast ruled lake, the low shore, the event kept small and far — and the red contour around the one figure quietly settles where the eye must go. The vertical smoke is the print's finest invention, a plumb line dropped through a horizontal world.

entries.title: The Gathering of the Manna
entries.shown: A crowd of Israelites in headbands and striped robes stoops across a dune valley, sweeping the pale ground for manna with bare hands; bowls and wicker baskets collect it, and one woman stands upright at center, a laden basket on her head, gazing out of the frame. Ridged hills rise behind under a strip of blue sky, and the fallen manna speckles the sand like coarse grain.
entries.quality: The print's structure is its virtue: a field of bent backs radiating around the one vertical woman, so the standing figure reads as the still center of the harvest. The hand-tinted flesh and drapery over crisp pen work give it the flavor of an old chromolithographed Bible plate, though the crowd's repeated stooping poses admit their shared origin.

entries.title: The Youth Among the Gazelles
entries.shown: Seen from behind, a curly-haired youth sits in the shade of a great wind-bent tree on a bluff, a thin staff planted beside him, one hand raised toward a group of gazelles that surround him — two at his shoulder, three more in the near foreground. Below the bluff a pale road switchbacks through a sunlit valley; the light comes from the open distance while the foreground stays in blue shadow.
entries.quality: The shade-against-glare structure is handled with real finesse — dense blue foliage and dark animals framing a bleached valley — and putting the viewer behind the boy, inside his shadow, is a quietly effective piece of staging. The gazelles are individually well drawn but crowd the sitter closely enough to strain the scene's wildness.

entries.title: The Evening of the Deluge
entries.shown: A vast pale vortex of moon and cloud fills the upper two-thirds of the frame, engraved in concentric whorls, with a flock of birds spiraling into the light; below, a calm sea, then a dark shore where a tent stands open with a fire and bottles inside, a red-cloaked figure stooping at its mouth, and pale animals — a waterfall pouring behind them — gathering at the right. The eye is pulled first and always into the luminous ring of sky.
entries.quality: This is the boldest translation in the set: Turner's dissolving light rebuilt as pure engraved line, the sky's circular hatching spinning the whole plate around its moon. The tiny warm-colored figure below is placed with cunning — one ember against the machine of the heavens — even if the foreground's inventory of tent, beasts, and cataract grows a little busy for a world about to drown.

entries.title: Sebastian Bound for Martyrdom
entries.shown: After Van Dyck: the young saint, pale and nearly nude with a white cloth at his hips, looks out at the viewer while a muscular executioner crouches to bind his ankles and a bearded soldier pulls his raised arm back overhead. Behind them crowd a white horse, helmeted men, and an upturned face, with one red banner glinting in the armor; a dog's grizzled head watches from the dark lower left.
entries.quality: The plate keeps Van Dyck's essential contrast — one smooth, luminous body set against a machinery of straining backs, horses, and steel — and the deep blue ink gives the crowd a genuinely nocturnal pressure. The saint's outward glance is the print's nerve; the surrounding melee is engraved so densely it verges on congestion.

entries.title: Christ in the House of Martha and Mary
entries.shown: A colored woodcut-style interior after Vermeer: Christ sits at right in a purple robe with a green mantle across his knees, gesturing toward Mary, who sits low at his feet in red bodice and white headcloth, chin in hand. Between them Martha leans over the white-clothed table to set down a basket of bread; light falls flat and even, and the eye circles the triangle of the three heads.
entries.quality: The print flattens Vermeer's early Baroque shadow into bold color fields with black-line hatching, closer to a fine chromoxylograph than to the painting, and the triangular composition survives the translation intact. The bread basket at dead center is exactly where the story's argument sits, and the colorist knows it.

entries.title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
entries.shown: After Vermeer: the girl turns over her left shoulder against a near-black blue ground, lips parted, in a blue-and-ochre turban whose long yellow lappet falls down her back; the pearl hangs in the shadow of her jaw above a white collar. The light comes from the left onto face and collar, and the eye goes where it always goes — eyes, mouth, pearl, in that order.
entries.quality: As a chromolithographic reduction of the most famous glance in painting it is honest work: the turban's blue and gold are struck in confident, visible strokes, and the dark ground is deep enough to make the head float. What the flat inks cannot do is the wet light in the eyes and pearl, and the print, sensibly, does not pretend otherwise.

entries.title: Girl in a Turban, with a Thread of Red
entries.shown: A second, longer version of the turbaned girl after Vermeer, showing more of her ochre jacket and shoulder as she turns against a scratched blue-black field; a sliver of red edges the turban above her brow, and the pearl catches a single white point in the ear's shadow. The lappet falls in broad cream-and-blue planes, and light models the face in soft, even tones.
entries.quality: The added shoulder gives the figure a torsion the tighter crop lacks, and the vertical tool-scratching in the dark ground lends the plate a worked, physical surface. The unexplained red edge at the turban is the printmaker's own liberty — a small vanity, but it wakes the whole color chord.

entries.title: Woman with a Pearl Necklace
entries.shown: After Vermeer: a young woman in a yellow, ermine-trimmed jacket stands in profile at right, hands raised to the ribbons of her necklace, facing a tall window at far left through which the light enters past a yellow curtain. Between them stretches a broad blank wall; below, a table heaped with dark drapery, a jar, and a powder brush holds down the shadowed foreground.
entries.quality: The engraver has grasped the painting's true subject — the empty, lit wall between woman and window — and has had the discipline to leave it almost untouched while hatching the foreground into near-blackness. That held emptiness against the massed dark is the print's quiet triumph; the profile itself is serviceable rather than tender.

entries.title: Gilles
entries.shown: After Watteau: the clown Pierrot stands full-length and frontal in his white satin suit — round hat, ruff, too-short sleeves, ribboned slippers — arms hanging, face blank and open. He is raised on a bank above four half-hidden companions: a straw-hatted pair, a red-capped man in red reclining at right, and a donkey's head with its rider glowering at lower left, all under halftone-dotted trees and sky.
entries.quality: Rendered in coarse halftone dots with one red intervention, the print turns Watteau's melancholy into something like an old theatre poster, and the trade mostly works: the white suit stays luminous because everything around it is screened darker. The dots blunt the famous face's ambiguity a little — softness becomes vagueness — but the lonely frontality, the whole point of the picture, is untouched.

entries.title: A Philosopher Lecturing on the Orrery
entries.shown: Eight figures crowd around a brass orrery in a darkened study, its arcing yellow rings framing two children who lean in at the machine's center, their faces the brightest passage in the frame. The light rises from a lamp hidden inside the instrument itself, so every face is lit from below; a grey-haired philosopher in a red robe presides from above, a note-taker works at the left, and a silhouetted man seen from behind blocks the source at the front. Bookshelves and a green drape sink into the near-black ground behind them.
entries.quality: A print after Wright of Derby that understands the original's central trick: hiding the light and letting the rings and faces carry it, so the eye circles the orrery exactly as the planets would. The under-lighting on the children is genuinely tender and the dark masses hold together well, though the outer figures stiffen into flat cutouts where the shadow economy runs thin.
